I confirmed no CI exists (no .github, no Makefile, no scripts, not a git repo) and no Info.plist file-sharing keys, and that no code reads the `unreadable-*` sidecar. I counted 107 `func test` across the bundle — the headline test count is accurate. WHERE I WAS WRONG AND CORRECTED MYSELF: I initially judged surf:lens-2's rung-5 corollary REFUTED, reasoning that a pending drop still on disk would make unpushablePendingCount non-zero; reading DropStore.swift:475-485 showed uploadingCount counts pending ids WITH a row, so unpushablePendingCount is exactly the reap's target set — the reviewer is right and I reversed my verdict. WHAT I REFUTED: seams-6's core mechanism (Firestore rules are stateless w.r.t. document history, so 'a revision that constrains recreation of a deleted id' is not rules-expressible and no assertion can pin it; B2 rests on SDK queue ordering + merge-upsert, which needs a client integration test, not a rules test). I also corrected surf:lens-4's harm attribution (the string is on the recipient's screen only; the sender never sees it) and downgraded surf:lens-1's headline harm chain (an atomic rewrite on a genuinely full disk also fails and returns early, keeping the journal — the destructive path needs a non-space sidecar failure). I did NOT re-report recorded residuals (probe-cap rotation, capability re-arm, serverTimestamp watermark, merge field-mask, single-field ownerUid stamp, SQLite outbox, the own-1 reap redesign, LocalDropStore.save silently dropping unreadable rows); where round 12 made one more dangerous I said so explicitly and scoped the finding to the new route (surf:lens-2). I did not manufacture findings to fill a quota: I hold three own-findings, one of which is a build-process gap and one a test-harness gap, both of which are causal for why rounds 11 and 12 each shipped new regressions inside their own fixes. D3: three of the four new regressions (remove's abort branch, redeem's persist-catch, redeem's recall-after-throw) live in branches with ZERO coverage, and I verified the two vacuity claims that matter — testRedeemNeverOverwritesAPendingLocalEdit (DropStoreTests.swift:855-884) forces the row pending via setFailAllSaves at :860 so it passes under the OLD predicate too and locks nothing about B4, and testAccountChangeResetsSyncEvidence (:842-851) drives a method production can no longer call.

ownFindings.title: The durable incident MEMORY retires on the first clean load, so a whole-file quarantine launders into the full all-clear after one new drop — own-B's premise is half-closed
ownFindings.trace: Round 12 built `hadLocalReadIncident` (DropStore.swift:440, written at :625-632, consumed at :642-653) so 'a destroyed library must never launder into a brand-new one'. Traced across launches: launch 1 corrupt file → LocalDropStore quarantines (:230-244), journals, and refresh sets the memory true (:627) → rung 4 (ProfileScreen.swift:103). User taps Dismiss → LocalDropStore.acknowledgeIncident (:263-278) does NOT match `if case .skippedRows?` for a whole-file quarantine, so it only clearIncident()s → the kicked refresh (:720) sees `.absentFile` (the file was MOVED to .corrupt-<ts>) → the switch's `default: break` keeps the memory → localProvablyClean false (:647-650) → latch stays false → 'Checking sync status…'. Correct so far. Then the user creates ONE drop: add() (:821-833) → LocalDropStore.save (:319-327) persists [drop] → the next refresh loads it cleanly → `.clean` → :629 sets the memory FALSE → localProvablyClean true → :654-656 latches → ProfileScreen.swift:152-156 'Synced — the server has confirmed your drops'. The memory is exactly as launderable as the journal it was built to outlive; it just costs one extra user action. No reviewer traced the quarantine path (all four marked incident-memory CLOSED, or PARTIAL for the unrelated .readFailed arm), and surf:lens-2 traced only the .skippedRows route.
ownFindings.harm: A user whose entire library is destroyed by a corrupt store file sees the banner once, dismisses it, pins one new drop, and from then on the Profile tab asserts positive server confirmation over a library that lost everything — no rung, no banner, no durable record anywhere. Same fabricated all-clear as surf:lens-2 but reached without any Dismiss-is-destructive behaviour, so fixing acknowledgeIncident alone does NOT close it. It also means the round-12 build note 'Dismiss can't launder a quarantine' overstates what shipped.
ownFindings.fix: The memory is a hole-plug for the absent-file window, not a record of loss; ship the positive record instead of strengthening the plug. (1) Land the surf:lens-2 `lostRowIDs` ledger and populate it for the quarantine path too — at quarantine time LocalDropStore knows the row count it could not read (it has the raw bytes), so record 'a library of unknown size was quarantined at <date>' as a durable fact, retired only by an explicit user Clear. (2) Retire `hadLocalReadIncident` on acknowledgement of a real loss record, never on a `.clean` load — a clean load proves the CURRENT rows read, which is not evidence about the destroyed ones (cross-cutting rule 4: the producing condition has not disappeared, only been paved over). (3) Keep the quarantine file's path in the record so a future recovery build has something to point at.

ownFindings.title: The gate that is supposed to protect the v3 rules deploy is unenforced: no CI, not a git repo, `npm test` is a manual step — and the lock it runs already fails open
ownFindings.trace: web/rules-tests/package.json:7 wires `node drift-check.mjs && firebase emulators:exec … "node rules.test.mjs && node deployed-rules.test.mjs"` and its own description says it 'MUST pass before any rules deploy (Wave A gate)'; firestore.rules:9-10 repeats the claim ('the emulator suite … MUST pass before any deploy'). I looked for the mechanism that enforces it: there is no .github/, no workflow file, no Makefile, no shell script anywhere in the tree (find over the repo, maxdepth 3), and the working tree is not a git repository at all — so no hook, no pre-commit, no PR check. The suite runs only when a human types it, and it additionally needs a local JDK + firebase CLI. Combined with seams-4 (the drift regex fails open on `let` and attributed properties, reproduced empirically) and with rules.test.mjs:95-97 hard-coding the reaction payload, the protection against the single change that would break every reaction after the v3 deploy is: one manual command, running one regex that misses the exact declaration form the next scheduled change uses.
ownFindings.harm: A documented safety claim with no mechanism behind it — the same defect class the wave charter is about, applied to the build instead of the UI. Concretely: the scheduled serverTimestamp watermark adds `@ServerTimestamp var commitAt: Date?` to DropReaction (ReactionService.swift:10-16); nothing forces the drift check to run, and if it does run it passes; the v3 deploy then makes every reaction write PERMISSION_DENIED at firestore.rules:78 → ReactionService.send throws (:70-73) → every viewer sees 'Couldn't send — it lives in this memory only' (MemoryScreen.swift:183) and the loop's entire payoff dies, with the counsel's own lock reporting green.
ownFindings.fix: (1) Put the repo under version control and add a single CI job (or, minimally, a committed `scripts/preflight.sh` invoked by the build) that runs `xcodebuild test` + `npm --prefix web/rules-tests test`; make it a stated precondition of the Wave A deploy checklist in DECISIONS.md so the gate is auditable. (2) Move the drift assertion into the device test bundle (own encoder-shape test, per seams-4) so it runs with the 107 tests that ARE routinely executed, and leave the .mjs check as a pre-deploy double-check rather than the sole guard. A lock nobody runs is a comment; a lock that runs in the suite the team already runs is a lock.

ownFindings.title: The test doubles reproduce production's isolation but not its failure modes, so every new abort/rollback branch ships uncovered — the structural reason rounds 11 and 12 each regressed inside their own fixes
ownFindings.trace: GatedCloudStore (DropStoreTests.swift:1218-1340) is exemplary: an actor with park/release continuations for saves, loads AND deletes, plus round-12's setUnackedRows (:1261, applied at :1315) faithfully reproducing per-row latency compensation. FlakyLocalStore (:1346-1390) is not: it has setThrowOnLoad and setFailDelete(ids:) only — NO save-failure knob, NO suspension gate on save or delete, and its acknowledgeIncident (:1358) merely sets `warning = nil`, reproducing none of production's round-12 destructive rewrite (DropStore.swift:263-278). Consequence, verified branch by branch: remove()'s new abort at :872-875 cannot be driven from any test (testDeleteDuringRefreshIsNotResurrectedByThePublish at :369-389 bumps the generation BEFORE remove, so the guard passes); redeem()'s persist-catch at :800-803 cannot be driven; redeem()'s post-throw recall gap cannot be driven; and every acknowledge test must use the real LocalDropStore, which is why the destructive-rewrite semantics were never exercised against a hostile filesystem. Three of the four new charter-class regressions in this round live in exactly those branches.
ownFindings.harm: Not a user-facing harm — a review-integrity harm, and the reason this wave keeps converging slowly: each round's fix adds a new early-return or catch path that no double can reach, so the next counsel round finds it by reading instead of the suite finding it by running. Cross-cutting rule 6 is satisfied in letter (the doubles are actors with real suspension points) and violated in effect (they cannot produce the failures the new code branches on).
ownFindings.fix: Extend FlakyLocalStore in the same round as the fixes it must lock: `setFailSave(ids:)`, `setGateSave/setGateDelete` + parked counts + releaseAll (mirroring GatedCloudStore's continuation pattern), and a `setJournalWritable(false)` mode; and give it an acknowledgeIncident that reproduces production's rewrite-or-keep-journal outcome so lens-1/lens-2 become testable without touching the real filesystem. Then adopt a standing rule for this wave: a fix that adds an early return, a catch, or a guard must ship with a test that ENTERS that branch — the counsel has repeatedly found that the guard, not the mechanism, is where the defect lands.

research.shipVerdict: NOT production-grade as it stands — but the gap is one short build round, not a redesign, and the shape of the remaining work is materially better than round 11's. What round 12 got right: of the 17 audited items I verify 12 fully CLOSED with non-vacuous tests (B2 staged-delete recall — mechanism verified against real SDK semantics, FirestoreAcked stages before the cancel and merge-set upserts behind the serialized delete; B4's single predicate; the additive phase-1 publish + cloudReadCompleted gate; per-row serverConfirmedIDs from hasPendingWrites paired with !isFromCache, which is exactly the right latency-compensation guard and whose double reproduces it; the delete-refusal taxonomy split, which is strictly safer than round 11 and correctly audited against delete-not-write semantics; server-only revocation of lastSyncError; the acknowledge rewrite's keep-the-journal-on-failure branch; the corrected Memory and ProfileScreen copy — 'sync is on hold' is gone from the entire tree, verified; the firstAt FIRST-IN badge; ShareDropSheet's liveDrop; the tri-state fetch itself, whose .absent has exactly one producer and cannot be fabricated client-side). The blocking problem is that four of round 12's own new mechanisms carry charter-class defects, and three of the four sit in branches no test can enter: (1) remove()'s new post-await guard keys on the global publish counter, so any concurrent refresh — including the scenePhase-.active refresh round 12 also added — silently abandons a delete after the disk row is already destroyed, leaving the Firestore document and every recipient's magic link live with no tombstone and no verdict; (2) the new cloudProvenIDs predicate treats a REFUSED write as proof the server holds the document, producing a permanent, unretirable 'the cloud copy may still exist' alarm for a document that never existed — which then masks every lower ladder rung for the life of the install, reopening the exact class round 10 closed; (3) the new uid gate on the receive flow replaced round 11's truthful failure with an unbounded, unlabelled, inescapable spinner on the app's entire acquisition path; (4) the new destructive acknowledgement, plus the reap and memory that retire on the same clean load, gives a one-tap (and, per my own-1, a one-write) path from 'N saved drops couldn't be read' to 'Synced — the server has confirmed your drops' over never-uploaded, now-destroyed drops. Each is a real regression against the charter's own words. The good news for scheduling: the four fixes are roughly 40 lines across DropStore.swift, ReceiveScreen.swift and ProfileScreen.swift plus the drift/test work, they are independent of each other, and — as in round 11 — none of them impugns the underlying mechanisms, only the wiring and the predicates. Ship after a round 13 that lands priority items 1–6 WITH the test-double capabilities (FlakyLocalStore save-failure knob and delete gate) so the abort/rollback branches stop shipping uncovered; that condition is not optional, because the recurrence of 'the fix contains the next defect' two rounds running is a coverage problem, not a reasoning problem.
research.waveExitAssessment: WAVE C CAN CLOSE AFTER ROUND 13 — one build round, then exit; a seventh review round is not warranted. Judged against the charter ('no silent data loss, no fabricated success, no reassuring copy the mechanics cannot back'), the wave has done its structural work: read/write provenance now gates every positive claim; verdicts are durable, per-object and revoked only by their issuing authority; ritual and receipt are separated; the honest-unknown state exists and is reachable on every surface; the deployed ruleset is pinned in-repo and the client's dependencies on it are asserted. What remains is not new mechanism, it is four wiring defects in round 12's own additions plus the copy fix — all named in the priority order, all small, all locally testable. Close Wave C when: (a) priority items 1–6 are built; (b) FlakyLocalStore gains the save-failure knob and delete gate and the three previously-unreachable branches (remove's abort, redeem's persist-catch, redeem's post-throw recall) each have a test that ENTERS them; (c) the durable loss ledger (lostRowIDs + a rung above 'Synced') exists, because 'a loss that leaves no record' is the last live instance of the charter's central failure; (d) the residual list is re-stated with the two items round 12 changed the risk profile of — the own-1 reap redesign (now one tap away) and the serverTimestamp watermark (now the exact declaration form the drift lock misses). Items 7–12 can close as recorded residuals with the existing ones. WHAT MUST PRECEDE LAUNCH REGARDLESS OF WAVE C: (1) The v3 rules deploy is the hard gate, and it is a SECURITY gate, not a polish gate — deployed-rules.test.mjs:61-64 pins, as currently passing, that any signed-in stranger can overwrite any drop document by stamping their own ownerUid. That is live in production today; every other launch item is subordinate to it. (2) Before that deploy: the reaction key/emoji drift protection must be real — the encoder-shape Swift test plus deriving the emulator payload from appReactionKeys(), because the first post-deploy reaction under a drifted struct is PERMISSION_DENIED → terminal verdict → the loop's payoff dies silently (own-2 + seams-4). (3) The deploy also un-blocks two things the client is currently paying for: ReceiveScreen's '.gone' verdict is presently UNPRODUCIBLE — a genuinely deleted drop shows the retryable 'check your connection' copy forever — and tombstone retirement is capability-latched to .denied, so proven-but-unresolved delete alarms cannot retire at all. Both are honest today and both should be re-verified the day v3 lands. (4) Privacy/App-Store surface: the 'One-time link' claim must be corrected before any public listing (surf:lens-4). (5) Account identity: anonymous-only auth with no retry and no SIWA linking means a lost token is a lost library; that is the recorded device-migration residual and it is a launch decision, not a Wave C one. (6) Process: put the repo under version control and enforce the test gate (own-2) — a Wave A deploy checklist whose preconditions run by memory is not a checklist.
